title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: When she went into Kitty's little room — a pretty, pink little room full of knick-knacks in _vieux saxe,_ as fresh, pink, white, and gay as Kitty herself had been two months earlier — Dolly remembered how they had decorated the room together the year before, with what love and gaiety. Her heart turned cold when she saw Kitty sitting on a low chair near the door, her eyes fixed unmoving on a corner of the rug. Kitty glanced at her sister, and the cold, rather ill-tempered expression on her face did not change.
"I'm just going now, and I'll have to stay shut in and you won't be able to come and see me," said Dolly, sitting down beside her. "I want to talk to you."
"What about?" Kitty asked quickly, lifting her head in alarm.
"What should it be, but your trouble?"
"I have no trouble."
"Nonsense, Kitty. Do you think I could fail to know? I know it all. And believe me, it amounts to so little... Each of us has been through it."
Kitty did not speak, and her face had a stern expression.
"He isn't worth your grieving over him," Darya Alexandrovna went on, coming straight to the point.
"No, because he's treated me with contempt," Kitty said, in a breaking voice. "Don't talk about it! Please, don't talk about it!"
"But who could have told you that? No one said that. I'm certain he was in love with you, and would still be in love with you, if it hadn't..."

"Oh, the most awful thing for me is all this sympathizing!" Kitty shrieked, suddenly flying into a passion. She turned round on her chair, flushed crimson, and, rapidly moving her fingers, pinched the clasp of her belt first with one hand and then with the other. Dolly knew this trick her sister had of clenching her hands when she was very excited; she knew, too, that in moments of excitement Kitty was capable of forgetting herself and saying a great deal too much, and Dolly would have soothed her, but it was too late.

"What, what is it you want to make me feel, eh?" Kitty said rapidly. "That I've been in love with a man who didn't care a straw for me, and that I'm dying of love for him? And this is said to me by my own sister, who imagines that... that... that she's sympathizing with me!... I don't want these condolences and humbug!"
"Kitty, you're being unfair."
"Why are you tormenting me?"
"But I... quite the contrary... I see you're unhappy..."
But Kitty in her fury did not hear her.
"I've nothing to grieve over or be comforted about. I am too proud ever to let myself care for a man who doesn't love me."
"Yes, I'm not saying that either... Only one thing. Tell me the truth," said Darya Alexandrovna, taking her by the hand. "Tell me — did Levin speak to you?"

The mention of Levin's name seemed to strip Kitty of the last remnant of self-control. She leaped up from her chair, and flinging her clasp on the ground, she gesticulated rapidly with her hands and said:

"Why bring Levin into this too? I don't understand what you're trying to torture me about. I've told you, and I'll say it again: I have some pride, and never, _never_ would I do what you're doing — go back to a man who has deceived you, who has loved another woman. I can't understand it! You can — I cannot!"

And, having said this, she glanced at her sister, and seeing that Dolly sat silent with her head sadly bowed, Kitty — instead of running out of the room as she had meant to — sat down near the door and hid her face in her handkerchief.

The silence lasted for two minutes: Dolly was thinking of herself. That humiliation she was always aware of came back to her with a special bitterness when her sister reminded her of it. She had not looked for such cruelty in her sister, and she was angry with her. But suddenly she heard the rustle of a skirt, and with it the sound of heart-rending, smothered sobbing, and felt arms about her neck. Kitty was on her knees before her.
"Dolinka, I'm so, so wretched!" she whispered penitently. And the sweet face, covered with tears, hid itself in Darya Alexandrovna's skirt.

As though tears were the indispensable oil without which the machinery of mutual confidence could not run smoothly between the two sisters, after their tears the sisters talked, not of what was uppermost in their minds, but, though they spoke of outside matters, they understood each other. Kitty knew that the words she had uttered in anger about her husband's infidelity and her humiliating position had cut her poor sister to the heart, but that she had forgiven her. Dolly for her part knew everything she had wanted to find out. She felt certain that her surmises were correct: that Kitty's misery, her inconsolable misery, was due precisely to the fact that Levin had proposed and she had refused him, and Vronsky had deceived her, and that she was fully ready to love Levin and to detest Vronsky. Kitty said not a word of that; she talked of nothing but her spiritual condition.

"I have nothing to make me miserable," she said, calming down. "But can you understand that everything has become hateful, loathsome, coarse to me, and I myself most of all? You can't imagine the loathsome thoughts I have about everything."
"Why, what loathsome thoughts can you have?" Dolly asked, smiling.

"The most utterly loathsome and coarse — I can't tell you. It's not unhappiness, or low spirits, but much worse. As if everything that was good in me was all hidden away, and nothing was left but the most loathsome. Now, how am I to tell you?" she went on, seeing the puzzled look in her sister's eyes. "Father just now began saying something to me... It seems to me he thinks all I want is to be married. Mother takes me to a ball: it seems to me she only takes me to get me married off as soon as may be, and be rid of me. I know it's not the truth, but I can't drive away such thoughts. Eligible suitors, as they call them — I can't bear to see them. It seems to me they're taking stock of me and summing me up. In the old days going anywhere in a ball dress was a simple joy to me, I admired myself; now I feel ashamed and awkward. And then! The doctor... Then..." Kitty hesitated; she wanted to add that ever since the change had taken place in her, Stepan Arkadyevitch had become unbearably repulsive to her, and that she could not look at him without the grossest, most hideous conceptions rising before her imagination.
"Oh well, everything presents itself to me in the coarsest, most loathsome light," she went on. "That's my illness. Perhaps it will pass."
"But you mustn't think about it."
"I can't help it. I'm never happy except with the children at your house."
"What a pity you can't be with me!"
"Oh, yes, I'm coming. I've had scarlatina, and I'll persuade mamma to let me."

Kitty insisted on having her way and went to stay with her sister and nursed the children all through the scarlatina, for scarlatina it turned out to be. The two sisters brought all six children safely through it, but Kitty was no better in health, and in Lent the Shtcherbatskys went abroad.
